title: Integrating agentic risk signalling in trusted research environments: Automating VEX with Agent2Agent protocols and model context protocol (MCP) in SACRO and TREvolution pipelines
abstract: • Proposes agentic VEX generation using Agent2Agent and Model Context Protocol • Embeds runtime traceability and exploitability logic in reproducible TRE pipelines • Automates vulnerability filtering and digital signing in SACRO-compliant systems • Supports federated reproducibility and schema validation for VEX artefacts • Enhances AI supply chain assurance with context-aware risk signalling This study presents a framework for automating the generation and validation of machine-readable vulnerability statements, known as Vulnerability-Exploitability Exchange (VEX) artefacts, within secure research environments. The work addresses a critical limitation in existing vulnerability reporting, where static scoring systems often fail to capture whether a flaw is truly exploitable in a specific analytic context. By integrating structured metadata capture, runtime instrumentation, and cryptographically verifiable provenance, the framework classifies vulnerabilities as affected, fixed, or not relevant, supported by machine-readable evidence bundles. The methodology was evaluated using containerised applications seeded with deliberately vulnerable components. Software bill of materials and vulnerability scanners were applied to generate baseline inventories, while reproducibility frameworks validated that results could be independently replicated. Findings demonstrate that automated VEX generation can reduce false positives by distinguishing theoretical from actionable risks, thereby improving security assurance and reproducibility in federated infrastructures. At the same time, the research acknowledges significant challenges. Computational overhead from multi-layered monitoring, dependence on external tools, and the risk of false negatives introduce barriers to adoption. Broader pilot studies across heterogeneous domains and benchmarking on standardised testbeds are required to enhance generalisability. Privacy concerns from extensive runtime monitoring and the need for sustainable maintenance models also demand attention. By combining automation with human oversight and aligning with emerging standards, the study contributes a reproducible, auditable, and context-sensitive approach to vulnerability management. The work provides both a proof-of-concept and a roadmap for refining security practices in sensitive computational environments.

title: YOLO-MARL: You Only LLM Once for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Advancements in deep multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) have positioned it as a promising approach for decision-making in cooperative games. However, it still remains challenging for MARL agents to learn cooperative strategies for some game environments. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent reasoning capabilities, making them promising candidates for enhancing coordination among the agents. However, due to the model size of LLMs, it can be expensive to frequently infer LLMs for actions that agents can take. In this work, we propose You Only LLM Once for MARL (YOLO-MARL), a novel framework that leverages the high-level task planning capabilities of LLMs to improve the policy learning process of multi-agents in cooperative games. Notably, for each game environment, YOLO-MARL only requires one time interaction with LLMs in the proposed strategy generation, state interpretation and planning function generation modules, before the MARL policy training process. This avoids the ongoing costs and computational time associated with frequent LLMs API calls during training. Moreover, trained decentralized policies based on normal-sized neural networks operate independently of the LLM. We evaluate our method across two different environments and demonstrate that YOLO-MARL outperforms traditional MARL algorithms.

title: On Thinking and Working Through a Pandemic
abstract: There are some things the pandemic didn’t change. I am still interested in doing scholarship; friends and colleagues have said that they are too. More than ever, I acknowledge the presence of the present in my approach to the past, having abandoned any conceit that what was going on around me had nothing to do with my choice of subjects or how I thought about them. Academics are embarrassingly well suited to lockdowns, being introverted by the requirements of their profession and possibly by nature: give us our research notes, books and articles, an internet connection, and a place with a closing door, and we have all we need to write. Even while I was teaching last spring—I am not teaching this fall—the shape of my days didn’t shift much. I had time. Yet other important things did change. A pandemic, even despite the considerable privilege of having a stable job, is limiting. Scholars cannot travel to archives and libraries. Conferences, including SHAFR, were canceled or migrated online, which meant that we lost access to some sessions and—more significantly, in my view—had no chance of the spontaneous conversations in hallways or bars that allow us to catch up with colleagues’ work and spark the best ideas. A pandemic is exhausting. Everyone I know says that it has been harder to think straight while worrying about their health and that of loved ones. Teaching online is tiring. There are reports of people sleeping more, worn out from anxiety or sadness or hours sitting at a screen. And pandemics are distracting. It is all very well to say that we have the resources and the time we need for our scholarship. But there is so much else to think about; as Wordsworth wrote, “the world is too much with us, late and soon.” We are overwashed with bad news, and it has not been possible for me, at least, to stop reading it and listening to it. How can we do our work when we are frightened and angry and cannot trust our national leaders to do anything right? The pandemic has brought lessons that both affirm and challenge my thinking and writing about history. The first of these concerns the role of fear in how people perceive each other, within and across borders. I have long admired the work on emotions of subfield colleagues Frank Costigliola, Barbara Keys, and Melani McAlister, who have described the ways in which American Christian evangelicals instrumentalized a discourse of fear to enhance their pursuit of religious freedom abroad through the deployment of U.S. policy.1 McAlister indicates by her examples that fear can be inspired by what is seen, or known; the Voice of the Martyrs and other groups made videos showing (or strongly hinting at) painful abuses of Christian bodies in order to display the persecution suffered by their co-religionists in Asia. Yet, often it is instead the unseen, the unknown, that inspires more powerful fears. The unwanted penetration or violation of the body by some invisible agent is one of the most basic of human terrors. As Joanna Bourke has argued, “the emotion of fear is fundamentally about the body—its fleshiness and its precariousness.” Fear of possession by spirits or ghosts was largely supplanted following the Enlightenment by dread of “unseen yet harmful microbes and bacteria,” with the assurances of science regarded at first as no more convincing than the promises of exorcist priests during an earlier era.2 My study of sensory encounters between the people of India and the Philippines and representatives of imperial states, British and U.S., confirms Bourke’s claim. Indians and Filipinos recoiled from “western” medicine, the gaze or the touch of a foreigner who promised to prevent them from getting a disease or to cure them of one they already had. Removing the sick to hospitals was tantamount to making them vanish. For their part, Britons, Americans, and other participants in empire worried that tropical pathogens, hidden in the swamps and jungles or (worse, they thought) concealed by dark-skinned bodies, might infect them without warning and thereby sicken or kill them. Hidden disease was identified with its dangerous Asian carrier. The unseen threat required visual manifestation if it was to be confronted. Thus, in matters of bodily safety, race told.3 Fears about COVID-19 are to some extent properly democratic: to viruses, all bodies would seem to look alike, and anyone can get infected. But in truth it hasn’t worked that way. Children are less susceptible than adults to getting sick. People of color—who make up a disproportionate number of essential workers, often live in multi-generational apartments or homes, and frequently lack access to health care—have contracted the disease and died from it well beyond what statistical models alone would suggest.4 And, despite clear evidence that the virus was transmitted to the East Coast of the United States primarily by travelers from Europe, U.S. President Donald Trump and others have insisted on labeling it “the Chinese virus” (“kung flu”) and persist in blaming its spread on the irresponsibility of Chinese hygienic practices and the mendacity of China’s leaders. The result has been an increase in the number of verbal and physical attacks on Asian Americans, including children.5 Thus is fear of a pathogen turned with demoralizing ease to racism—a move historians recognize all too well.6 A second lesson of our experience with the coronavirus, and likely the most obvious to historians of U.S. foreign relations, is the global nature of the pandemic—the very definition of which suggests its worldwide reach and strength. Viruses have no regard for national boundaries. They are carried on bodies that move from place to place, and perhaps even on substances that are touched again and again before they arrive where they are going. (Is there anyone reading this who did not or does not disinfect their hands after bringing in the mail?) In this way, we are reminded that the best work of the current generation of historians also moves fluidly, naturally, across borders. I have returned to scholarship that reminds me of this: Sven Beckert’s book on cotton, Erez Manela’s global history of Wilsonianism, Petra Goedde on international peace movements, Matthew Connelly on world population control, Mary Sarotte’s 1989, and many others.7 I have picked up for the first time accounts of the flu pandemic of 1918.8 The spread of the coronavirus, and even more stories about the effort to find a vaccine to prevent it, remind me of the Hungarian polymath Michael Polanyi’s claim that there exists a “Republic of Science,” an idea captured by Richard Rhodes’s magisterial history of the atomic bomb. Science, according to Polanyi, is by its nature a borderless pursuit. “The authority of scientific opinion remains essentially mutual,” Polanyi wrote. Scientists are meant to share data without regard to national borders, visit each others’ labs, publish in the same journals, and meet at international conferences. The thought that a discovery might be confined to a single nation state or private entity is antithetical to the nature of science.9 Scientists may regard this as an axiom, or may have done so in the past. Governments and pharmaceutical companies do not, so we witness efforts to nationalize the hunt for a coronavirus vaccine. I am of two minds concerning this tension. A vaccine is not a bomb. At this writing, companies, funded by governments and sometimes working with universities, are moving ahead with sizable human trials of vaccines. Their formulas are different, and it seems likely that having a variety of approaches aimed at combatting the virus will serve humanity best. If some efforts fail, it will be good to have others that might work. Immunologists in all labs have some understanding of which sort of vaccine—whole virus, genetic (DNA or RNA), viral vector, protein-based—their rivals are working on, so this is a competition that is to an extent open source. Is it likely that a single, international lab, one (say) based in Geneva and run by the World Health Organization, could have done as well as this less centralized approach? As ever, scientists struggle to balance the claims of their international Republic against those of their employers and political leaders.10 A third lesson of the pandemic that is relevant to my scholarship, past and future, has to do with the importance of culture in understanding the human response to life under the virus. I have long been interested in the role of culture, broadly defined, in shaping U.S. foreign relations. It has seemed to me that we miss something meaningful about the ways in which nations and people interact if we neglect those factors that affect the ideas and feelings policymakers deploy as they work, their values, religious beliefs, emotions, and prejudices concerning especially race and gender, their ways of apprehending others through every bodily sense, their understanding of gesture and language, even their grasp of rituals and symbols, theirs and others. Such factors shape the interests of states: perceptions of national security have something to do with how people imagine borders and read threats. The anthropologist Clifford Geertz has most strongly influenced my thinking on these matters, even as I acknowledge the elusiveness of his definition of culture, which he characterizes, by turns and in one book alone, as “webs of significance” spun by human beings, a “set of control mechanisms—plans, recipes, rules, instructions,” and a “historically transmitted pattern of meanings embodied in symbols, a system of inherited conceptions expressed in symbolic forms by means of which men [sic] communicate, perpetuate, and develop their knowledge about and attitudes toward life.”11 Whatever the perils of wrestling with so elastic a concept, culture nevertheless, in my view, tells us a good deal about the world’s response to the coronavirus. The physician and writer Atul Gawande has made this point. Describing efforts—mostly successful—to prevent the virus from overtaking his hospital, Mass General Brigham, in Boston, and the senior living facility nearby where his mother lives (less success there), Gawande lists a familiar first “four pillars” of effective response: hygiene, screening, distancing, and wearing masks. But the fifth, and “arguably most difficult” pillar to establish, he says, is culture. It is possible, he says, to get people “to focus on safety and freedom; keep me safe and leave me alone.” Those are easy enough to imagine. But what is needed in addition is a cultural (and ethical) shift that involves people understanding that measures they may take will keep others safe. They must affirm values of altruism, of the importance of community as well as individual health.12 Geertz’s social “control mechanisms,” his “recipes,” must in this case be recognized and, if need be, changed. There are indications of both success and failure in the quest to create and sustain a culture of community welfare, and they take me back to the lessons of globalism. Some nations have done far better than others controlling the impact of the virus. In East Asia, where masks are often worn against pollution, seasonal allergies, or other airborne illnesses, governments have managed on the whole to contain the worst ravages of COVID-19. Elsewhere, wearing masks has been stigmatized as cowardly or creepy, and it has been harder to convince people to put them on. (Speculation that East Asians have also been successful at virus containment because they social distance naturally are less persuasive, seemingly sprung from stereotypes about Chinese dynastic fears of conspiracy or Japanese resistance to intimacy. We need to be careful with culture.)13 Those governments that have managed to inspire public trust have on the whole fared better than those inclined to authoritarianism, by system or the personality of their leaders.14 Many believe that it is no accident that governments led by women—Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand), Angela Merkel (Germany), Tsai Ing-wen (Taiwan), and Sanna Marin (Finland)—have managed to contain illness and reduce death.15 It is armchair commentary, perhaps, but it is hard to avoid the conclusion that something about the gender expectations assigned to male and female leaders has made this more than coincidence. The kind of community thinking described by Gawande might just be more common among women, and the empathy required of leaders in times of distress may be more available to those unattached to such masculinist behaviors as supreme self-confidence, posturing, and top-down modeling. There is another lesson, one applicable to the field of history generally rather than to the study of foreign relations alone. That is an appreciation for contingency, the claim that all events, causes of events, and ideas, are conjoined with other events, causes, and ideas. John Lewis Gaddis has written that the fundamental difference between doing history and doing laboratory science is the absence in the first of these of “independent variables.” For historians, all variables are dependent, or as Gaddis puts it, “interdependent.” Everything significant hinges on everything else. That is a prescription for indeterminacy, which is no doubt frustrating to those who seek simple answers to historical questions. (It does not mean that truth is ineffable or nonexistent, just complicated.)16 Through this pandemic, I have been surprised that so many of my colleagues, some of whom are historians, seem to expect certainty where it cannot exist. They were quick to indict university administrators for guessing wrong, however briefly, last spring about whether to send students home immediately and how to move fully to online classes. They demanded to know in early May precisely what the university planned to do in late August. They wanted answers, now—clear-cut ones. As a historian, this seemed to me folly. Historians know better than to think that they can predict the future, having failed, for the most part cheerfully or resignedly, to settle on single explanations for past events. If we cannot agree on how to define the U.S. empire (or even, in some cases, whether the United States was an empire), why it took so long for the United States to intervene militarily in the two world wars, and why the nation went to war in Vietnam at all, how can we be surprised or angry that administrators—at a liberal arts college anyway, men and women much like ourselves, but with somewhat nicer clothes—cannot give us straightforward answers to questions concerning how the university should cope with an unprecedented pandemic, especially when the modes of virus transmission, the role of hard surfaces and aerosols, and the importance of “viral load,” for example, are so poorly understood? Administrators gather evidence and make their best judgments—just as historians do. Yes: there is a lot of money at stake for universities. But to assert that campus decisions are all predicated on money is rather like saying that the reason for everything the United States has done (or not done) in the Middle East over the past century is oil: it’s true, but insufficient as an explanation. This brings me to a final lesson of the pandemic. If historians acknowledge the importance of contingency in confronting the virus, as they acknowledge it in their own approach to research, it must follow that they conduct themselves with humility when they do their scholarship. We live, and work, with uncertainty. “History imbues us with agency and with possibility,” according to Drew Gilpin Faust, the historian and president emerita of Harvard. “But I also derive from history a sense of profound humility—in face of what others have confronted in our differing circumstances but common struggle to chart a path through a challenging world.”17 We are imperfect creatures, able to get things right just so often, and only to the best of our abilities. As David Lowenthal has observed in another context, “it is salutary to be reminded that we are perforce fallible not only epistemically but also personally, subjugated not only to our slippery subject matter but to our slippery selves. To the genre's own insuperable limitations––data that are always selective and never complete; the unbridgeable gulf between actual pasts and any accounts of them; bias stemming from temporal distance, from hindsight, and from narrative needs––we must add, and keep in mind, human frailty.”18 This, for me, is the lesson of living in a pandemic and writing history. The limits of our understanding match the limits imposed on us by the virus; we are necessarily reminded of our vulnerabilities as scholars and human beings. Andrew J. Rotter is Charles A. Dana Chair of History at Colgate University, where he has taught since 1988. He is author most recently of Empires of the Senses: Bodily Encounters in Imperial India and the Philippines (New York, 2019). He is currently writing a book on the cultural approach to U.S. foreign relations history.

title: Editorial: Plant-based lipids for sustainable food products
abstract: science will play in shaping the next generation of resilient, nutritious, and sustainable food systems.Lipids contribute fundamentally to food texture, creaminess, lubrication, flavor perception, and stability, while also influencing processing performance and consumer acceptance. In many food systems, the functionality of lipids extends beyond nutrition and plays a decisive role in determining product structure and eating quality. Conventional animal derived fats such as butter, lard, and tallow have historically provided desirable sensory and functional properties in numerous food applications. However, the environmental burden associated with livestock derived lipids, including greenhouse gas emissions, land utilization, feed production, and intensive resource consumption, has intensified interest in identifying sustainable alternatives. Consequently, transitioning toward plant based and alternative lipid sources represents an important strategy for reducing the environmental footprint of modern food systems while simultaneously supporting nutritional and technological requirements. The increasing demand for sustainable foods has also stimulated significant innovation in lipid structuring technologies. Unlike traditional liquid oils, many plant derived lipids lack the physical and structural properties necessary to mimic solid fats used in bakery products, confectionery systems, dairy alternatives, and meat analogs. Therefore, researchers are increasingly exploring methods to engineer plant-based lipids into structured systems capable of replicating the rheological and functional behavior of conventional fats. Such approaches are essential for improving texture, stability, sensory performance, and consumer acceptance of next generation plant-based foods. Moreover, advances in lipid structuring offer opportunities to reduce saturated fat content while maintaining desirable product quality attributes. This research topic presents several studies that collectively demonstrate how plantbased lipid systems can be engineered, stabilized, and functionally optimized for sustainable food applications. A major advancement emerging from this collection is the development of structured lipid systems designed to improve oxidative stability and functionality. Polyunsaturated fatty acid rich plant oils are highly susceptible to oxidation because of their unsaturated chemical structures, necessitating innovative stabilization approaches during food formulation and storage. Lipid oxidation remains one of the most important challenges limiting the commercial utilization of highly unsaturated oils because it negatively affects flavor, color, nutritional quality, and shelf life.One contribution addressed this challenge through the formulation of structured margarine derived from perilla seed oil using enzymatic interesterification combined with rosemary extract as a natural antioxidant. At an optimized concentration of 1500 ppm, rosemary extract substantially reduced peroxide values and secondary oxidation products, exhibiting antioxidant performance comparable to synthetic antioxidants such as TBHQ. This work highlights the growing potential of plant derived antioxidants to replace synthetic additives while improving the sustainability and clean label characteristics of lipid-based foods. More importantly, the study demonstrates how multifunctional formulation strategies can simultaneously improve nutritional quality, oxidative stability, and consumer appeal. The replacement of synthetic antioxidants with naturally derived compounds also aligns with broader industry trends emphasizing transparency, ingredient simplicity, and consumer driven product development.Another important theme within this issue is the emergence of naturally structured lipid assemblies such as oil bodies, oleogels, oleosomes, and emulgels as alternatives to conventional emulsifier-based fat systems. These systems offer opportunities to mimic the texture and functionality of solid fats while utilizing healthier unsaturated oils. Naturally occurring lipid assemblies have attracted considerable interest because they can provide structural stability without extensive processing or the addition of synthetic emulsifiers and stabilizers. Such systems may also improve ingredient compatibility and contribute to the development of minimally processed foods with enhanced functionality.Zhang and coworkers developed a peanut oil body based nutritional emulsion system capable of accommodating higher lipid and carbohydrate contents while maintaining enhanced stability. Unlike conventional emulsions dominated by coalescence, the peanut oil body systems primarily exhibited controlled flocculation behavior with lower polydispersity and improved resistance to destabilization. The naturally occurring oleosin proteins located at the oil water interface contributed significantly to emulsion stability without requiring synthetic emulsifiers. This study highlights the remarkable potential of biologically derived lipid assemblies as functional and sustainable alternatives for the formulation of next generation food products. Such systems may play transformative roles in clean label formulations and plant-based alternatives to traditional lipid rich foods.The issue also explores multifunctional lipid soluble bioactives for food preservation applications. One study investigated oregano essential oil as a natural preservative for pasteurized milk. Oregano essential oil, rich in antimicrobial compounds such as carvacrol and thymol, effectively inhibited microbial growth and delayed oxidative deterioration during refrigerated storage at concentrations as low as 2 mg/L.further demonstrate the potential of plant derived lipid soluble bioactives as multifunctional preservation agents. Importantly, this work also highlights practical regulatory considerations associated with incorporating natural preservatives into commercial food systems across different geographic regions. As consumer demand for naturally preserved foods continues to increase, plant derived essential oils and bioactive lipids may become increasingly important components of sustainable food preservation strategies.Beyond technological innovation, this research topic includes a broader perspective on the societal and nutritional discourse surrounding dietary fats. Meijaard and coworkers challenge the oversimplified vilification of fats, particularly saturated fats, by examining evidence from global nutrition studies and meta analyses. Their work emphasizes that sustainability assessments of lipid systems must consider not only environmental impacts, but also nutritional adequacy, accessibility, affordability, economic realities, and cultural dietary patterns. This perspective is particularly important because sustainable food systems cannot be evaluated solely on environmental metrics without considering their implications for public health and societal acceptance. The review further discusses emerging lipid alternatives and evolving consumer perceptions regarding dietary fats, reinforcing the importance of adopting holistic and systems level perspectives in future lipid research and policy development.Collectively, the studies included in this research topic reveal several converging trends in sustainable lipid science, including the development of multifunctional lipid systems integrating structure, nutrition, and oxidative stability; increasing utilization of natural antioxidants and bioactive compounds as alternatives to synthetic additives; growing interest in biologically derived lipid assemblies such as oil bodies and oleogels; and recognition of the need for holistic evaluations encompassing environmental, nutritional, societal, and economic dimensions of lipid sustainability.Together, these advances demonstrate that plant-based lipids are not merely substitutes for animal fats, but sophisticated engineered systems capable of enabling the next generation of sustainable food products.We sincerely thank all contributing authors for their valuable and high-quality research contributions. We also extend our gratitude to the reviewers for their rigorous evaluations and constructive feedback, which significantly strengthened the quality of this collection. Finally, we appreciate the support and guidance provided by the editorial team at Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems throughout the editorial process. It has been a privilege to serve as Guest Editors for this research topic. We hope this special issue will inspire continued innovation at the intersection of lipid science, sustainability, and food system transformation, ultimately contributing toward the development of healthier and more resilient global food systems.

title: Adversarial Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models: A Critical Review and an Adaptive Multi-Layered Defense Framework for Enterprise AI
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now sit at the centre of many digital services, supporting the generation, summarisation, interpretation, and use of natural-language and multimodal information. As these models are connected to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external tools, cloud platforms, enterprise knowledge bases, and autonomous agents, the security boundary extends well beyond the model itself. This article critically reviews adversarial vulnerabilities across the wider LLM ecosystem using peer-reviewed studies, influential preprints, and authoritative standards available up to July 2026. It examines prompt injection, jailbreaks, data and model poisoning, backdoors, model extraction, membership inference, training-data extraction, RAG manipulation, supply-chain compromise, multimodal attacks, and the misuse of agentic tools. Current safeguards, including reinforcement learning from human feedback, adversarial training, prompt and output filtering, retrieval validation, differential privacy, red teaming, and explainability, reduce some risks but remain inadequate against adaptive and multi-stage attacks. In response, the article introduces the Adaptive Multi-Layered Adversarial Defense Framework (AMADF), a ten-layer enterprise architecture covering identity and access management, prompt sanitisation, retrieval provenance, semantic threat detection, secure inference, explainability-based risk scoring, output validation, human review, continuous monitoring, and governance. AMADF draws on Defense-in-Depth, Zero Trust Architecture, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, Explainable AI, and socio-technical security principles. It offers organisations a practical structure for designing, assessing, and governing secure LLM deployments, although its effectiveness still requires empirical testing in operational environments. Keywords: Large Language Models, adversarial machine learning, prompt injection, jailbreak attacks, retrieval-augmented generation, AI agents, Zero Trust, Explainable AI, trustworthy artificial intelligence, cybersecurity.

title: Research on an Intelligent Query Mechanism for BIM Multi-Source Heterogeneous Information Based on Large Language Models and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
abstract: The entire lifecycle of construction engineering involves a vast amount of multi-source heterogeneous data. The fragmentation of this data leads to problems in traditional query methods, such as semantic conflicts, difficulties in cross-phase collaboration, and data silos. While IFC standards, BIM platform APIs, and traditional database integration methods have made some progress in the integrated management of BIM and multisource information, they suffer from weak dynamic correlation capabilities, low levels of semanticization, and rigid query interfaces. The management of multi-source heterogeneous data in the construction industry faces a full-process technical demand, ranging from the automatic parsing and fusion of multi-modal data, to semantic association and knowledge construction, and further to natural language-based intelligent queries and service encapsulation. Based on this, this paper constructs an intelligent query mechanism based on Large Language Models (LLM) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Firstly, a construction domain knowledge graph is built by parsing multi-modal data to provide a knowledge base support for queries. Secondly, the LLM enables human-computer natural language interaction, parsing user query intent and planning it into an ordered MCP tool call chain. The MCP then completes the calls to external data resources, knowledge bases, and tools. Finally, the LLM organizes the results and returns them to the user. This achieves natural language interaction, deep semantic association, and precise intent understanding for multi-source heterogeneous data in construction engineering, supports result traceability, and lowers the barrier to query usage.

title: A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models
abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) trains large language models with teacher guidance on student-generated trajectories, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the histories encountered during deployment. As its use expands across language model training, different formulations of supervision and optimization make it difficult to compare methods and understand when they are effective. This survey develops a unified view of OPD through the interplay between student-generated states, teacher information, and policy updates. This framework connects the foundations of distillation with self-distillation, multi-teacher integration, reinforcement learning, and interactive agents. We examine how these settings change the supervision available to the student and relate the resulting design choices to capability transfer, training efficiency, and deployment. Our synthesis centers on the conditions under which guidance remains reliable and learnable as the student evolves, considering both immediate performance and the capacity for subsequent learning. We conclude by discussing open challenges in adapting supervision and allocating computation to support effective learning.

AI Agents for Cloud Reliability: Autonomous Threat Detection and Mitigation Aligned with Site Reliability Engineering Principles
abstract: Cloud environments face constant cybersecurity threats, requiring efficient and reliable defense mechanisms to ensure service continuity. This paper presents a novel approach leveraging AI agents to autonomously detect and mitigate threats in cloud systems, aligned with Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices. Using the NSL-KDD dataset, we train AI models to classify attack types accurately, achieving high precision and recall, particularly with Random Forest classifiers. We further simulate threat scenarios to measure the AI agent’s response times, comparing Time to Detect (TTD) and Time to Mitigate (TTM) against traditional methods. Results demonstrate a significant reduction in TTD and TTM, with the AI agent achieving up to 6x faster detection and mitigation. This autonomous capability not only improves threat response but also supports SRE-aligned metrics such as Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR), ensuring enhanced reliability in cloud infrastructures. By integrating AI-driven automation into cloud security operations, our findings underscore the potential of AI agents as proactive security operators, advancing both cybersecurity and operational resilience. This research contributes to the development of scalable, autonomous solutions crucial for the future of secure, resilient cloud computing.

title: Corrosion and Chemical Agent Destruction
abstract: Supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) is a developing technology for the destruction of hazardous and nonhazardous wastes. General Atomics and its subcontractors are currently conducting two comprehensive research and demonstration programs geared toward the destruction of Department of Defense (DoD) wastes utilizing SCWO technology. Wastes of primary interest include chemical agents and solid propellants. Corrosion testing performed in support of these programs identified platinum and titanium as candidate reactor construction materials. Kinetics testing emphasized chemical agent destruction. Kinetics results for chemical agents show destruction and removal efficiencies for GB, VX, and mustard agents to be in excess of 99.9999%, limited only by detection capability.
